lead: Joseph Mallord William Turner, known during his lifetime as William Turner, was an English Romantic painter who is regarded as one of the greatest British painters of the 19th century.
paras: Turner painted weather as a physical event, and he did it with some of the newest and least permanent pigments of his day. Some of what he put down has faded, so the pictures we see are quieter than the ones he exhibited.
His career runs from careful topographic watercolors to canvases that are almost pure light.

chapters.title: Watercolor and the picturesque
chapters.text:
Turner entered the Royal Academy schools as a teenager and made his early living from watercolors of abbeys, castles and bridges. They are built from thin washes of {{Powder Blue}}, grey and {{Straw}}, with a tonal range that stays calm.

He soon began to exhibit oils, in which he borrowed the golden light of Claude Lorrain and the dark storm skies of Dutch marine painters.

chapters.title: Italy, Venice and the new yellows
chapters.text:
His first visit to Italy, in 1819, opened a new range of color. In Venice, which he painted on later visits in the 1830s and 1840s, sea, sky and marble merge in pale gold, {{Pink}}, and {{Turquoise}}.

He used the new pigments available in his lifetime, among them chrome yellow and {{Cobalt Blue}}, alongside {{Vermilion}}, {{Carmine}} and lead white. Some of his reds and yellows were not light-fast, which is a particular problem in the watercolors.

A frequently told story says that on a varnishing day at the Royal Academy in 1832 Turner added a small red buoy to a grey seascape beside Constable's brightly colored picture. The details are reported by later writers, so treat it as tradition.

chapters.title: Fire, steam and light
chapters.text:
The Fighting Temeraire of 1839 shows a pale ship tugged to its breakup against a sky of {{Orange}}, {{Apricot}} and {{Gold}}. Rain, Steam and Speed of 1844 builds a train out of dark paint in a yellow-grey mist.

In late works such as Norham Castle, Sunrise, from about 1845, subject almost disappears and the whole picture is yellow, blue and white. Many of his late canvases were not exhibited in his lifetime.

He died in 1851 and left a huge body of work to the nation.

chapters.title: What our archive shows
chapters.text:
Our archive holds 648 of his works, in oil and watercolor. His darkest large areas are {{Smoky Black}} and dark brown, and his lightest are {{Light Ivory}} and {{Ecru}}, the warm white of his skies and paper.

He uses black and {{Bistre}} less than other painters of his period. These are photographs of varnished oils and fading watercolors, so the true values may be both lighter and bluer than they appear.
